text:
In August 1854, cholera tore through Soho, a crowded, working-class district of London. Within about ten days, more than five hundred people living near Broad Street had died. Cholera is a disease that causes violent diarrhea and vomiting, and it can kill within a day by draining the body of water. In those days nobody knew what caused it, and the dominant theory held that it spread through "miasma", foul-smelling air rising from rot and filth.

John Snow, a physician who lived a short walk from Broad Street, did not believe it. Snow was already well known for pioneering the use of anaesthesia: he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He had also been thinking about cholera for years. During the epidemic of 1848 and 1849 he had noticed something that the miasma theory could not explain. Cholera attacked the gut first, not the lungs. If people were breathing in a poison, why did the illness begin in the stomach and bowels? Snow reasoned that sufferers must be swallowing something, and that the disease then multiplied in the intestine and left the body in the patient's waste. If that waste reached drinking water, it could infect others. He had published this idea in 1849, but few took it seriously. He had no microscope evidence and no way to prove it. The outbreak on Broad Street gave him a chance to find proof.

Snow began where any good investigator would, by going to the scene and asking questions. He walked the streets and knocked on doors. He wanted to know who had fallen ill, where they lived, and what they had been drinking. At that time, most households had no running water at home. People collected it from public pumps in the street, and Soho had several. Snow noticed that the deaths clustered tightly around one of them: the pump on Broad Street, near what is now the corner with Lexington Street.

To make the pattern visible, he drew a map. On a street plan of the neighbourhood, he marked each death with a short black bar at the address where it had occurred. The bars piled up around the Broad Street pump like a swarm. Maps showing disease were not entirely new, but Snow used his to make an argument, and it was a persuasive one.

A skeptic could still say that the pump was simply in the middle of the worst neighbourhood, so Snow looked for exceptions, which are often more revealing than the rule. A workhouse, a charitable institution housing the poor, stood close to the pump. It held about five hundred people, yet only five had died. Snow learned that the workhouse had its own well on the premises, so its residents had no need to use the Broad Street pump. Nearby, a brewery employed seventy workers, and none of them died. The brewery also had its own well, and the men were allowed free beer as part of their pay, so they hardly drank water at all.

Then there were the strange cases at the other extreme. A woman who lived far away in Hampstead died of cholera. Snow discovered that she had once lived in Soho, and that she liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had it carried to her home every day. Her niece, who drank from the same supply, died as well. No one else in her area fell ill.

By the beginning of September, Snow was convinced. He took his evidence to the local board of guardians, who were responsible for the parish. On 8 September 1854 they agreed to remove the handle from the Broad Street pump, which made it impossible to draw water. The outbreak was already fading by then, since many residents had fled the district and the number of new cases had begun to fall before the handle came off. For that reason, historians have debated how much the removal itself changed anything. But the removal was a symbol of the new idea, and Snow's real work was just beginning.

He kept investigating, and he eventually found the likely source. A baby had died of cholera at 40 Broad Street in the days before the outbreak, and the family's waste had probably drained into a cesspool leaking close to the well beneath the pump. A local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who had at first doubted Snow, joined the search. He helped trace the first cases and confirmed the link to the baby. In the end, Whitehead became one of Snow's strongest supporters.

The official response was less welcoming. A government inquiry concluded that the evidence was not convincing, and the miasma theory kept its hold for years. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, without seeing his ideas accepted. Only later, as the germ theory of disease took hold and the cholera bacterium was identified, did his work receive full recognition.

Today Snow is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations. His method was simple: gather the facts, map them, look for the cases that break the pattern, and let the evidence guide you.
